content: Acacia berlandieri, also known as Berlandier Acacia, Guajillo Acacia, guajillo, or huajillo, is a shrub that is native to the Southwestern United States. It belongs to the Fabaceae family, commonly referred to as the bean family. This plant typically grows to a height of 1 to 5 meters and produces spherical, white blossoms that bloom between February and April. The species name berlandieri is derived from Jean-Louis Berlandier, a French naturalist who conducted studies on the wildlife of Texas and Mexico. Acacia berlandieri contains a diverse array of alkaloids, which are chemical compounds that can have significant biological effects. The plant is known to cause toxic reactions in domestic animals, particularly goats. Due to its toxicity, it is not suitable for use as forage or fodder for livestock. The alkaloid profile of Acacia berlandieri is notable for its complexity. Among the most abundant alkaloids identified in this plant are N-methylphenethylamine, tyramine, and phenethylamine. A recent study identified a total of 31 alkaloids in samples of the plant's foliage. Remarkably, this includes trace amounts of five amphetamines that were previously thought to be synthetic compounds: amphetamine, methamphetamine, N,N-dimethylamphetamine, p-hydroxyamphetamine, and p-methoxyamphetamine. In addition to these amphetamines, other trace alkaloids found in Acacia berlandieri include DMT (dimethyltryptamine), which is commonly present in related plant species, nicotine, and mescaline. Mescaline is typically associated with cacti and is rarely found in other types of plants. The same group of researchers later reported detecting most of these alkaloids in another plant species, Acacia rigidula, at a concentration of 66%.
